name: Skin flaying astringent lotions

card.summary: Caustic lotions reported in colonial-era Jamaica that peeled the skin in order to lighten complexion.
card.note: Documented to cause painful skin loss; part of a broader history of harmful skin-lightening products.

quick.overview:
In the colonial era, some women in the Caribbean used harsh astringent lotions intended to lighten the skin. Accounts of Jamaican women describe lotions that caused painful flaying, meaning the outer skin was stripped off, with the goal of a paler complexion.

The practice belongs to a long history of skin lightening, in which colonial hierarchies, slavery and caste tied lighter skin to status. Its appearance goal was a lighter complexion; its documented result was injury.
quick.how: Descriptions are historical and general: a corrosive or astringent liquid was applied to the face or body, causing the surface layer to blister and shed. No instructions are given here.
quick.risks: Historical reports describe painful skin loss. Skin-lightening agents more broadly are linked to mercury poisoning, ochronosis from hydroquinone, steroid-related skin thinning and greater vulnerability to sun damage and infection.

lead: Skin flaying astringent lotions were harsh caustic or astringent preparations used in colonial-era Caribbean societies to lighten the skin. Wikipedia's history of skin whitening records that Jamaican women used astringent lotions that caused painful flaying, alongside cashew nut oil that burned the skin of Caribbean women and vegetable mixtures that gave painful reactions to women in Suriname.[1]

They sit within a longer story: European immigrants brought lightening recipes to the colonies, where they blended with Indigenous and West African herbal traditions, and colonial rule tied lighter skin to status, a link historians connect to slavery, caste and colonial hierarchies.[1]

angle.text: Users sought a lighter complexion by stripping the outermost skin. The documented outcome was painful injury rather than a reliable change in tone.

paras: Skin lightening is old: Egypt and Greece used honey and olive oil, while Greek and Roman cosmetics used white lead and mercury, which eroded skin, and Elizabethan Europe used Venetian ceruse, a lead and vinegar mixture.[1] In the United States in the 1800s lead-, arsenic- and mercury-based products were used, and marketing to Black women grew in the Jim Crow era.[1]

Lead and arsenic products were linked to hair loss, skin corrosion, paralysis and lead poisoning; mercury to neurological and kidney problems; hydroquinone to ochronosis and patchy depigmentation; corticosteroids to skin atrophy and fragility.[1] Lightened skin is described as more vulnerable to sun damage and infection.[1]
South Africa began banning mercury or high-hydroquinone products in the 1970s; the Black is Beautiful movement and health awareness slowed sales in the 1960s.[1]

timeline.event: Arsenic complexion wafers advertised in the US.[1]
Black is Beautiful movement slows skin-lightening sales.[1]
South Africa begins banning mercury and high-hydroquinone products.[1]
